TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
THURSDAY, 09 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 3, DAY 8
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH MATT SHERMAN AND DAVID ROWE,
COUNSEL ASSISTING
BORA KAPLAN SC WITH KATHLEEN HEATH, COUNSEL FOR THE
COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA
NAOMI SHARP SC, COUNSEL FOR THE STATE OF NEW SOUTH WALES
NICHOLAS BENDER SC, COUNSEL FOR THE MAINSTREAM JEWISH
BODIES
MATT COLLINS AM KC, COUNSEL FOR THE AUSTRALIAN
BROADCASTING CORPORATION
LUKE CHAPMAN, COUNSEL FOR THE SPECIAL BROADCASTING
SERVICE
JEREMY GILES SC, COUNSEL FOR JILLIAN SEGAL AO

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you, Commissioner. Before I call Ms Segal, I note
that the witnesses appearing today are from organisations who are newly represented
at the bar table and I ask them to announce their appearance.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Well, Ms Segal is giving evidence for the second time.
There's no need to re-swear Ms Segal.
DR COLLINS AM KC: Commissioner, my name is Collins I appear for the
Australian Broadcasting Cooperation.
COMMISSIONER: Mr Collins, my apologies.
MR CHAPMAN: If it please the Commission, my name is Chapman. I appear for
SBS.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Thank you, Mr Chapman.
MR GILES SC: And Giles for Ms Segal again.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you. Very well.
<JILLIAN SEGAL AO, ON FORMER OATH
MR LANCASTER SC: Ms Segal, you are, of course, the Special Envoy to Combat
Antisemitism.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You prepared your first statement dated 30 April this year
and you have prepared a further statement dated 30 June 2026.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Are the contents of that statement true and correct?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I tender that statement. The document ID is
STAT.8999.0001.0426.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the statement will be received as an exhibit.

MR LANCASTER SC: When you gave evidence during Hearing Block 1, you
explained your own professional background, your appointment to your current
office and, in broad terms, the work of that office. I won't ask you to repeat that now,
but I will address immediately your Plan to Combat Antisemitism which was
released on 10 July 2025, a year ago tomorrow; correct.
MS SEGAL AO: Important day, yes, thank you.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, that plan contained 13 focus areas of action for
combatting antisemitism?
MS SEGAL AO: It did.
MR LANCASTER SC: And one focus area was culture, arts and public
broadcasting?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in your statement, your second statement just tendered,
at [7], you note that between October and December last year, you developed
a supplement to the plan which is titled “Implementing the Special Envoy's Plan to
Combat Antisemitism: Action Plan for Government”.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, I did.
MR LANCASTER SC: You delivered that Action Plan to the government in
January 2026?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And part of that Action Plan relates to the media?
MS SEGAL AO: It does.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you've annexed that part of the Action Plan to your
statement as Annexure B, haven't you?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And just to confirm, before you have given evidence today,
have you reviewed statements provided by the ABC Editorial Director and the ABC
Ombudsman?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. In your Plan - and I can go to it, if you wish,
but can I just -

MS SEGAL AO: The Action Plan or the Plan-plan?
MR LANCASTER SC: The Plan.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: It's STAT.8999.0034.0005. On page 11 of the Plan, which
is page 13 of the PDF, you say this:
"Culture shapes perception. Publicly funded institutions like arts festivals, galleries
and public broadcasters must uphold antidiscrimination values and be accountable
for the narratives they promote. While freedom of expression, particularly artistic
expression, is vital to cultural richness and should be protected, funding by
Australian taxpayers should not be used to promote division or spread false/distorted
narratives."
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the statement, your second statement to the Commission,
in particular paragraphs 30 and 32, I will just address two parts of those paragraphs
with you. In paragraph 30, you say:
"The ABS and SBS are public broadcasters with statutory obligations - over and
above their professional responsibility - to present news and information accurately,
impartially and objectively. They occupy a particularly significant in Australian life,
shaping national discourse and cultural norms."
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, that's correct, in my opinion.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in paragraph 32 you have said in your statement:
"The editorial priorities and decisions of the ABC and SBS have far-reaching
impacts on the Australian psyche, our national discourse/outlook and accepted
'truths', noting that they are Australia's 'most trusted news brands'."
That's your understanding?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your statement does refer to private media here and there,
but it's fair to say your focus is on the role of the public broadcasters; is that right?
MS SEGAL AO: My focus in the statement or my focus generally?
MR LANCASTER SC: Both.

MS SEGAL AO: Certainly, it's the focus of the statement. I think my focus is on
both. I think they're both important. I think that, as I said, the ABC and SBS are the
most trusted brands and they are watched by many, and are opinion makers and,
therefore, I think it's very important. And I - some of the evidence that was given
before this Commission by one of your experts last week also made it clear that
young people were increasingly listening to the ABC and SBS, so I think they're very
important. And they have - because of their public funding, they have additional
responsibilities set out in their charters.
So that's why I think they also have a special responsibility. But I do think
commercial media is also extremely important and I make that point in my statement,
and I have continued to meet with them as well as, obviously, with the SBS and
ABC.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have referred in your statement to the - what you
describe as the unique duties and obligations placed on public broadcasters, and you
are referring there to the statutory character of many of those duties and obligations?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, to take the ABC and its statute as the first example,
do you have in mind the following types of obligations? One is the obligation of the
ABC under its charter in section 6(1)(a) of the Act to provide comprehensive
broadcasting services of a high standard?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is another that you have in mind that you consider it's
important to note the ABC is obliged under its charter to provide an independent
national broadcasting service, and the statute refers to that in one of the sections?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Another subsection requires the ABC to take account of the
multicultural character of the Australian community?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And there's an obligation imposed by statute on the ABC's
Board in section 8(1)(b) to maintain the independence and integrity of the ABC.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes. But I think that section 8 also references an obligation to
make sure that the reporting is accurate.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. If we could bring up 8(1)(c) that's a statutory
obligation on the Board of the ABC:

"To ensure that the gathering and presentation by the [ABC] of news and
information is accurate and impartial according to recognised standards of objective
journalism."
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, I think that is a very important subsection.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Act also provides in section 79A that, subject to the
Act, it's for the ABC to determine to what extent and in what manner political matter
or controversial matter will be broadcast?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And just to run through some of the key statutory
obligations on the SBS, to ask you the same question, whether these are the duties
you have in mind as the unique ones you referred to. The SBS legislation has also
a charter in section 6(1) and it provides that the SBS:
"...is to provide multilingual and multicultural broadcasting and digital media
service that inform, educate and entertain all Australians, and, in doing so, reflect
Australia's multicultural society."
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: There is a legislative obligation on the SBS's Board under
section 10(1)(a) of the SBS Act to maintain the independence and integrity of the
SBS; right?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And comparably to the ABC statute, SBS's statute says in
section 10(1)(c) that SBS must ensure:
"...that the gathering and presentation ... of news and information is accurate and is
balanced over time and across the schedule of programs broadcast."
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Finally, in the SBS Act, section 70A provides that - again,
comparably to the ABC's legislation - SBS is to determine:
"...to what extent and in what manner political or controversial matter will be
broadcast by the SBS."
So, a further affirmation of the independence that the legislature intends.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you have made a number of recommendations in
your statement, and I will come to those in a moment. But just at a broad level,
several of them - this is your paragraph 44. Several of them expressly propose new
ways of ensuring that public broadcasters comply with their statutory obligations; is
that right?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is it fair to say that your approach to the public broadcasters
is that you want long-established standards upheld, rather than proposing changes to
those underlying standards?
MS SEGAL AO: Absolutely.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I address some of the matters that you have raised in
respect of the ABC. And in paragraph 33 of your statement, you've said that many in
the Jewish community are concerned by what they view as public broadcasters'
disproportionate, misleading or factually incorrect coverage of issues relating to
Israel and the conflict in the Middle East. They're reports that have been given to
you; is that right?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And paragraph 34 - this is just to identify what the criticism
is that you are bringing forward. Paragraph 34, you said - I won't read it all out, but
you refer to a “common and pervasive perception” among the Australian Jewish
community?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And further in that paragraph, you have referred to
coverage lacking balance, the conflict in Gaza being overemphasised relative to other
global conflicts, disproportionately giving voice to anti-Israel perspectives which
exacerbated the prevalence of antisemitism in Australia and the conflation of Jewish
identity with the State of Israel.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, read literally, your paragraphs advance some pretty
serious criticisms; do you agree?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes. But I'm happy to explain them in further detail.
MR LANCASTER SC: I'll give you that opportunity in a moment. But the
criticisms reported to you from the Jewish community are, is this right, based on
anecdotal evidence from various members of the Jewish community who have come
to you?

MS SEGAL AO: Yes. Yes. I mean, part of my role is obviously to advise
government, but in order to advise government, I need to consult with the Jewish
community, the community that is experiencing the antisemitism, and understand
their concerns and where they are drawn from, as well as then to consult with others,
with government and government agencies, and to be informed by the work that I
have done also with overseas envoys. We can talk about that as well.
MR LANCASTER SC: Those criticisms - would you agree, it's difficult to test
propositions when they are expressed at that level of generality?
MS SEGAL AO: Well, exactly. But they are a perception and a very strongly held
perception from the Jewish community, that the way in which the Gaza conflict in
particular and the activities that are going on in the Middle East are reported have
created an impression of great negativity about Israel, and that there is this conflation
antisemitism that I think we discussed in my first appearance here.
And it should not, I think, be dismissed, okay, because it's a very serious perception
that a community under attack here in Australia feels that the trusted national
broadcaster is not presenting the situation in the Middle East in a way that they think
is not biased and accurate. And my contention is that if you look - I think I sort of
detail it further in - I'll just tell you the paragraph.
MR LANCASTER SC: I will certainly be coming to -
MS SEGAL AO: There are many ways in which that happens, okay. It's not just that
they come out negatively, but it's when the news story is run, where in the broadcast,
how long the focus is, what other stories about other conflicts are covered, what the
person who is the reporter actually says. So it's a complex impression, matters that
go to that impression, but it is clearly held by the community and my contention is
there is that concern.
We therefore have to - as you said, it's very hard to test, okay. But there are methods
to test it that have been set up, complaints, et cetera, and my contention is that that
whole system is not working to assure all of us that the reporting is as per required.
And that's why I make the suggestion of an oversight exercise, a standing committee.
MR LANCASTER SC: I'll certainly ask you about the complaints procedure. Can
I just ask you about a couple of the phrases you have used in paragraphs 33 and 34.
You refer to the coverage of the conflict in the Middle East being disproportionate or
overemphasised relative to other global conflicts. Now, of course, I take it you accept
that conflict in Gaza is a significant geopolitical event. I don't think any of us would
doubt that.
MS SEGAL AO: Sure.

MR LANCASTER SC: Many people in Australia of various origins do have ties to
the region and are touched by the conflict? Do you agree?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Many others, even without connection to anyone in the
region, have an interest in the history and politics of that region.
MS SEGAL AO: Sure.
MR LANCASTER SC: And do you accept that the ABC could not be criticised for
considering that it has an obligation, given its statutory responsibilities, to give
a substantial measure of attention to a conflict of that significance?
MS SEGAL AO: Absolutely. I'm not in any way suggesting that they shouldn't
cover the matters that they consider important. But there are also lots of important
issues around the world. There are major famines. There are other wars that we don't
hear about at all in Africa. There are, you know, other major global concerns. And
during the period that we are speaking of, the Gaza conflict, it's the perception of the
Jewish community feeling constantly that they are being faced with reporting about
the Middle East, about Gaza, and about Israel in a way that paints Israel constantly in
a negative light.
And I think that there's not an understanding - my view is that the reporters and the
hierarchy of the ABC don't have an understanding of the conflation issue, and that is
what I think we can correct. I say later that we can correct that with a bit of
education, which hasn't happened. I believe it would help to actually understand that,
through the IHRA definition. I think it's a good tool. It's not seeking to control what
people say and do, but it's an education tool. And I just don't think they have that
understanding.
COMMISSIONER: How would the application of the IHRA tool bear relevantly on
the extent to which the ABC covered the Gaza hostilities?
MS SEGAL AO: It wouldn't. It wouldn't impact the extent. It would make - enable
the reporters to understand better, I think, the conflation because it would be, are you
seeking to make the point so much that Israel is different in its fighting of the war to
other wars that have been fought by Australia, by America, et cetera, that that
conflation risk is there for Jewish Australians?
So it would just help them in the understanding of it. I don't think it would in any
way reduce necessarily the reporting. The reporting, I think, has to be an
understanding just of that type of antisemitism. I just don't believe that they have
a full understanding of that.
COMMISSIONER: I think it's fair to say that in the United States, the United
Kingdom and Canada, there has been a deal of media concentration on the war in

Gaza, and the image of Israel has suffered in all those countries, as well as in
Australia.
MS SEGAL AO: Absolutely.
COMMISSIONER: So is the suggestion that the broadcast media in all those
countries suffers from some bias?
MS SEGAL AO: Well, I think that we have a growing situation of appreciation of
that problem in the UK, if I can give you an example. Because I think a lot of the
ABC coverage from time-to-time sort of follows the BBC coverage or uses BBC
stories and information. And that's not a criticism of the ABC in any shape or form.
Stories come from different quarters.
But the BBC has a different structure of oversight, and it has a very strong regulator
over it, Ofcom, which has very different powers to ACMA here. And I know we are
straying a little bit but, okay, to answer the question. And Ofcom has powers to open
their own investigations. They can look at a story and direct the BBC to take it down,
to look at things differently. They can fine the BBC. They had an own-motion
investigation into BBC reporting on Gaza, which was the second element that they
looked at.
You might recall there was a lot of publicity here about their investigation in relation
to a story concerning President Trump and the way that had been cut and different
parts of the story put together. But, anyway, the investigation was into that and into
the Gaza reporting. And Ofcom - this was in November '25. Ofcom found that the
coverage was incorrect, was not accurate; that they had, for example, shown the
starving child. We had seen the similar story here on the ABC, when it was
well-known that that child was not in that situation because of lack of food but had
an illness, unable to absorb food.
And they found that it was so inaccurate and it was part of the way that they were
portraying Israel that - and similarly the Trump story - and as a result of that
decision, publicity, et cetera, the Director-General of Ofcom resigned because he
took it so seriously that they had this obligation of accuracy and balance.
So we don't have that structure here where there is a strong regulator looking over
and, of its own-motion, assessing and testing and reporting. So complaints - and
I know we will come to it, but complaints go through a process in the UK as they do
here, but Ofcom reports every fortnight on the complaints. So there's much more
monitoring.
COMMISSIONER: Ms Segal, I interrupted Mr Lancaster's examination, and I feel
you might have strayed a little bit in answer to my question, so if we can go back to
Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: I think we’ve moved right to the end of the examination.

MS SEGAL AO: If you want to save time, we've tried.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I take you back a little.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, sure.
MR LANCASTER SC: Just to address one of the other ways that you express the
common perceptions that have been relayed to by the Jewish community. And it's
described by you as the ABC disproportionately giving voice to anti-Israel
perspectives.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, in your statement at paragraph 43, you do indicate
that it's not your contention that the ABC and SBS should be expected to take a more
pro-Israel or less anti-Israel position. So that is your view?
MS SEGAL AO: Per se, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can you provide an example from what has been reported
to you of a public broadcaster taking an anti-Israel perspective. What does that
actually involve?
MS SEGAL AO: I think rather than any specific - I mean, I do focus in on one
specific example. I'll just find the -
MR LANCASTER SC: If you are referring to the -
MS SEGAL AO: In 38 - 35, sorry. But, see, the difficulty, Mr Lancaster, is if you
take one specific example, people go, "Oh, but this could be this. It could be that."
It's the - I'll talk to the specific example, but it is the overriding quantum of
everything, and where it's placed and the emphasis. But let me talk about this
specific example.
MR LANCASTER SC: I was going to raise that example with you in a moment. I
was just concerned to understand what an anti-Israel perspective is in terms of the
complaints that have been made to you about the public broadcaster's coverage.
What does that -
MS SEGAL AO: That is an anti-Israel example.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. So something critical of Israel's actions; is that an
anti-Israel perspective?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes. Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: And so the concern expressed to you is that there have been
a disproportionate number of coverage or stories that are critical of Israel?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes. And when you look at the stories that are critical of the other
parties like Hamas, the terrorist organisation, et cetera - I mean, what we have been
seeing is a war, okay, between one country that was attacked and is then defending
itself and attacking back, and another country. So there are going to be examples on
both sides of activities in a war which is always, you know, very sad for everyone
involving unfortunate loss of life. But it's the preponderance of the focus that
community has conveyed to me of the focus on the behaviour of Israel as opposed to
the behaviour of Hamas.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. I take it you also agree it's very difficult to assess that
proposition objectively without a substantial examination of a great number of news
broadcasts over a period of time?
MS SEGAL AO: Absolutely. And that, as I spoke earlier, is what Ofcom did. It
looked at it overall. And that is what my contention is, that we should - it's not an
attack on anyone or on the ABC, but it's almost, Mr Lancaster, that I would like - I'm
hearing from important stakeholders of mine how concerned they are, how aggrieved
they are, how they feel that their trusted broadcaster is not being fair and accurate.
I would like the ABC to be as good as it possibly could be, okay, not in any way to
restrict it or constrain it from being independent, but just to be as good as it could be.
And I do think a structure where an independent group of people look at what is
happening and they can give it a huge tick, or they can give it guidance as to the fact
that it needs to understand this particular hatred we're focused on better.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have indicated earlier that you have seen the statement
prepared by the Editorial Director of the ABC, Mr Gavin Fang.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: He addresses the ABC's coverage of the 7 October terrorist
attack and the war in Gaza in his statement; you would have read that?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And I can take you to it, if you like, but in paragraph 57,
what he said is that:
"The ABC has taken particular care to ensure that a wide variety of relevant
perspectives have been fairly represented. The organisation has been criticised by
both supporters of Israel and critics of Israel. The ABC has not sought to adjudicate
between competing political or legal claims, but has instead focused on robust
journalism, including careful question, appropriate challenge of interviewees while
avoiding the expression of editorial opinion."

Do you accept that the ABC does seek to take care to ensure that a wide variety of
relevant perspectives have been represented in its coverage?
MS SEGAL AO: That is not something that I have turned my mind to as to
assessing that. That's what I'm seeking to have an oversight committee do, and can
I just take the point, because you referenced it: I don't think looking at a balance of
complaints - because he references, "We've had complaints from both sides or from
all sides about - and that probably tells us we have got it right because everybody is
complaining". I don't think that is the right way to judge whether it's actually being
fair.
Different communities make complaints. The Jewish community is a very, very, very
small percentage of this community. If there are almost equal number of complaints
from the Jewish community, it's a disproportionate number of members of the Jewish
community who are feeling pretty aggrieved. And I think that if the ABC has taken
particular care, if this is all true, then what harm is there in having an independent
committee look at the overall reporting? I do not see what harm it does.
It doesn't in any way detract from their independence. In fact, it might give them an
extra verification, an extra boost that what they are doing is absolutely fine. It's just
that it may not be fine, okay. It wasn't fine in the BBC, okay? And I just don't know
how you can think or how they think that they can set the rules, which are their
standards; they can review them, which is their internal complaints system - it's an
Ombudsman but it's internal, appointed by the Board, reporting to the Board; and
they can mark their own homework.
I mean, they are, with respect, judge, counsel and jury. They are all of it. And I'm
just saying, I don't think anyone accepts the fact that you can always mark your own
homework. You can have this view, and I'm sure it's genuinely held, and I don't
accuse any individual in the ABC of not holding a genuine view. But I think having
an assessment just would be important for everyone in our community.
MR LANCASTER SC: I'll come back to the position of the ABC Ombudsman in
a minute, but as you've indicated, you appreciate the Ombudsman reports directly to
the Board of the ABC?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that the ABC Ombudsman is distinct from the editorial
function; in other words, the Ombudsman does not act or report to the editorial
division?
MS SEGAL AO: No, but the Ombudsman does report to the Board and is appointed
by the Board.

MR LANCASTER SC: The Ombudsman, when she issues a report, is - and making
a conclusion about some editorial decision involved in coverage by the ABC, the
Ombudsman isn't marking her own homework in that context, is she?
MS SEGAL AO: Well, she is looking at the editorial policies and judging against
the editorial policies of the ABC. Okay. She is not looking at things in a broader
context. She is just saying do they satisfy those policies. And, no, she is not marking
her own homework; she is marking the ABC's homework. But she is part - albeit she
doesn't report to the director of news, she is still part of the ABC and part of the
culture of the ABC.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I just take you back to an observation you made about
the fact that, as I think you are aware, ABC and SBS both do receive complaints
about, in some instances, the same news article or the same coverage from different
perspectives. You appreciate that that happens?
MS SEGAL AO: I'm - I believe it does, yes, but - yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I just take you to a couple of documents just to show
you. So ABC.5999.0001.0207. This is in the year to 31 October 2023. So PDF page
2.
MS SEGAL AO: This is from the Ombudsman?
MR LANCASTER SC: This is just a report on complaints relating to the
Israel-Gaza conflict and it is an Ombudsman report to the Board.
MS SEGAL AO: Mm-hm.
MR LANCASTER SC: If you could just zoom in on the section at the foot of the
page. There's a reference to 573 complaints, 89 per cent of which claimed the
coverage was biased or lacked balance. Do you see that?
MS SEGAL AO: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: 52 per cent claimed Hamas or Palestine was favoured and
47 per cent claimed Israel was favoured. So that's a documented example of what
you're referring to happening, namely, complaints from each side in substantial
proportions.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, but as I said, Mr Lancaster, I don't accept that equal numbers
of complaints means that you've got the story right. You can have the story very
wrong and a lot of people from different perspectives would be complaining. I don't
think it proves the fact that there's accuracy. I mean, you know, the example in my
statement of an inaccurate story of a report from the United Nations saying - or a
United Nations spokesperson saying that a significant - if I just turn to

it - a significant number of children were going to die in the next - 14,000 were going
to die in the next 24 hours.
It's a significant statement. It was wrong, okay. The ABC - BBC knew it was wrong
and apologised and had very significant coverage of the fact it was wrong. The claim
was actually clarified by the BBC before the ABC started reporting it. They reported
it all day and left it online for a significant - for a whole week.
It painted Israel, as I said, into a very negative light. The Ombudsman did find it was
incorrect; they breached the Editorial Standards. But there were a lot of complaints
about it. I'm sure lots of complaints from the community - I'm sure there were
complaints from other people too. That doesn't in any way mean that the reporting
was accurate and that it didn't give a negative impression of Israel, because it did.
MR LANCASTER SC: I'm going to take you to that example that you've addressed
in your statement you've just referred to in a moment. Before I do, can I take you to
a second document from the Ombudsman to address this point again.
MS SEGAL AO: Sure.
MR LANCASTER SC: It's ABC.5999.0001.0139. This is the 20 January 2026
Ombudsman's mid-year update, and on the first page, in the second
paragraph - complaints about - the sentence, to be clear this was - complaints about
content broadcast on the ABC platforms increased to 3043 for the six-month period,
dominated by concerns about the Middle East. Most related to bias or lack of
balance, with 51 per cent of the audience concerned ABC content was broadly
pro-Palestine, 47 per cent believing the coverage was pro-Israel. So it's another clear
documented example of that feature that we've referred to.
MS SEGAL AO: Yes, but as I said, you don't know where these complaints are
coming from. And I don't know. But if the 51 per cent believing it was too
pro-Palestinian came from - or pro-Palestine came from the Jewish community, it's
a very small part of the community, and if 47 believing it was pro-Israel and
depending where they came from, it's a much larger part of the community. So
I don't think that the balance tells us anything other than a lot of people are watching
